transcript.text: LG GSXV91BSAE showing Er FF and the freezer is only about -8. There's a scraping noise and frost on the back wall inside. Help!

On LG fridge freezers, Er FF means the freezer fan fault: the control board has spotted the fan inside the freezer isn't spinning as it should. That fan blows air over the cooling coil behind the back panel, so when it struggles the freezer warms up, which fits your -8°C. The scraping noise and the frost on the back wall point to the most likely cause: ice building up behind the panel until the fan blade catches on it. That usually happens when the automatic defrost isn't clearing the frost (a defrost heater or sensor problem), or when warm air is getting in past a door. Less likely, the fan motor itself is wearing out. The checks below tell these apart. 1. Look at the frost and listen to the fan. Open the freezer and hold the door switch in by hand for 20–30 seconds. If you hear the fan whirr and then a scrape or tick, the blade is hitting ice, so the cause is ice build-up rather than the motor. If there's thick ice on the back wall and the fan is silent, ice has probably jammed it. A thin dusting of frost with a silent fan points more towards the fan motor.
2. Do a full manual defrost. Switch it off at the wall, move the food into cool boxes or a neighbour's freezer, put towels down, and leave the doors open until every bit of ice has gone. That can take 12–24 hours, because ice behind the panel melts slowly. Don't chip at it or use a hot-air gun. Then dry it, switch it back on and give it several hours to cool.
3. Check the door seals while it's off. Run your fingers round the freezer seal for splits, gaps or a section that has come away, and check nothing stops the door shutting flat, such as the ice tray, a drawer or packaging. What the results would mean. If the code and the scraping go after the defrost and it gets back to about -18°C, ice was blocking the fan. Keep an eye on it for the next few days, though. If the frost and noise come back within days to a week, the defrost system isn't working and needs repairing; defrosting only buys time. If the fan is still noisy or the code returns straight away with no ice present, the fan motor is the likely culprit. On your food: at -8°C things may still be solid but aren't being kept safely frozen for long. Anything that has thawed soft is best used or thrown away rather than refrozen. I can't tell how thick the frost is, it's just frost on the back wall. The only noise I hear is the scraping/ticking, no proper whirring. I can't leave it off for 24 hours as I've got nowhere to put a full freezer of food, and I'm worried about it sitting at -8. Could I do a shorter defrost overnight, maybe 6-8 hours, with the food wrapped in towels?

Yes, a shorter overnight defrost is a sensible compromise, and it's worth doing. It may not clear every bit of ice hidden behind the back panel, so the problem could come back sooner than after a full defrost. But if it melts the ice around the fan, it should get the fan spinning again and the freezer cooling properly in the meantime. What you're hearing fits that picture. A scrape or tick with no proper whirr usually means the fan is trying to turn and its blade is catching on ice. That points to ice build-up rather than a dead motor, though it doesn't rule the motor out completely. To get the most out of 6–8 hours:
1. Speed the melt up safely. With it switched off at the wall and towels down, put a couple of bowls or pans of hot (not boiling) water on a folded towel inside the freezer and close the door. Swap them for fresh hot water every 30–45 minutes. Steam melts the ice much faster than leaving the door open, and it won't harm the plastics. Don't use a hairdryer or heat gun, and don't chip at the ice.
2. Protect the food. Pack it tightly together in cool boxes or strong bags, with ice packs or frozen bottles of water if you have them. Wrap the lot in towels or a duvet and keep it somewhere cool, away from radiators. A dense, well-wrapped pile of frozen food holds its cold far better than separate items. Because it's starting at about -8°C rather than -18°C, check it in the morning: anything still hard with ice crystals is fine to go back in, but anything soft right through should be used soon or thrown away, not refrozen.
3. Before you switch back on, wipe out the water and check the small drain hole at the bottom of the back wall is clear. A gentle trickle of warm water should run away freely. A blocked drain can cause exactly this kind of ice build-up. Afterwards, give it a few hours with the doors shut, ideally before you put the food back. What the result would tell us:
• Fan sound comes back and the code goes: ice was blocking the fan.
• Frost and scraping return within a few days to a week: the automatic defrost isn't working, and that needs repairing (usually the defrost heater, its thermostat/sensor or the control). Further defrosts would only buy time.
• Code stays on, or there's still no whirr even with the ice gone: the fan motor itself becomes the more likely fault. Both of those repairs mean taking the back panel off and getting into

Ok, I can do that overnight. The assistant's message cut off though, you said both repairs mean taking the back panel off and getting into... what? I won't be removing any internal panels myself, just so you know.

Sorry about that. The end of the sentence was: both repairs mean taking the back panel off inside the freezer and getting into the area behind it, where the cooling coil, the fan and the defrost parts sit. That involves disconnecting wiring and working right next to the cooling pipes, which are easy to puncture, and a puncture usually writes the appliance off. So it's an engineer's job anyway. You're right not to remove any internal panels, and nothing I'm asking you to do needs it. Your part is just the overnight defrost and then watching what happens: 1. After it's been back on for a few hours, hold the freezer door switch in and listen. A smooth whirr with no scraping, and the Er FF code gone, means ice was jamming the fan. Keep an eye on it over the next week.
2. If the frost and ticking come back within days, the automatic defrost isn't working. The usual causes are the defrost heater or its thermostat/sensor. An engineer would test those.
3. If the code stays on or there's still no whirr even with the ice gone, the freezer fan motor becomes the more likely fault. When you book an engineer, tell them about the code, the scraping, and whether it came back after defrosting. That points them straight to the fan or the defrost parts. It's also worth checking whether the fridge is still under LG's guarantee or any extended cover you bought, as that could make the repair free.
